courses.title: Crypto Fundamentals
courses.blurb: Wallets, tokens, DEXs, rugs, market cap, on-chain basics — the bedrock every survivor needs.

lessons.title: Liquidity Pools
lessons.intro: Most Solana DEXs (Jupiter routes, Raydium, Orca) are AMMs: every trade pulls from a Liquidity Pool — a smart contract holding two tokens — instead of matching an order book. LP providers earn fees from every swap. A few on-chain DEXs (OpenBook, Phoenix) still use order books, but you keep your own keys either way.

concepts.def: A smart contract holding two tokens (e.g. SOL/USDC) that traders swap against.
Someone who deposits tokens into a pool and earns a share of every trading fee.
Usually 0.25-1% per swap, split proportionally among all LP providers.
When token prices diverge, your pool share shifts — you may end up with less than just holding.
Automated Market Maker — the algorithm that prices trades based on pool ratios instead of order books.

questions.q: What do liquidity providers earn?
questions.answer: A share of trading fees
questions.why: LP providers earn a cut of every swap fee. The more volume through the pool, the more you earn.

questions.q: What is Impermanent Loss?
questions.answer: Value loss when token prices diverge vs. just holding
questions.why: IL happens when the price ratio of your pooled tokens changes. It's 'impermanent' because it can reverse if prices converge.

questions.q: What does a Liquidity Pool replace?
questions.answer: A traditional order book
questions.why: AMM-style DEXs (most of them) use liquidity pools instead of a traditional order book — though a few on-chain DEXs like OpenBook and Phoenix still run one.

questions.q: What is an AMM?
questions.answer: An algorithm that prices trades based on pool ratios
questions.why: AMM stands for Automated Market Maker. It uses a mathematical formula to price trades based on the ratio of tokens in the pool.

questions.q: If a pool has equal value of SOL and USDC, and SOL price doubles, what happens to an LP provider?
questions.answer: They experience impermanent loss vs just holding the two tokens
questions.why: When prices diverge, the AMM rebalances the pool automatically. You end up with less of the token that went up and more of the one that didn't — impermanent loss.

lessons.title: Rugs & Scams
lessons.intro: In crypto, a rug pull is when devs drain liquidity or dump tokens, leaving holders with worthless bags. Knowing the red flags is your first line of defense.

concepts.def: Devs remove all liquidity or dump tokens suddenly, crashing the price to zero.
LP tokens locked in a time contract — proves devs can't pull liquidity early.
The wallet that deployed the token. Large allocations here = major red flag.
A contract that lets you buy but blocks selling. You're trapped the moment you enter.
Manipulating people psychologically to gain trust before executing a scam.

questions.q: What is a honeypot token?
questions.answer: A contract you can buy but not sell
questions.why: Honeypots are coded to block sell transactions. Once you buy, your funds are stuck. Always test with a small amount first.

questions.q: Why is a liquidity lock important?
questions.answer: It means the dev can't remove liquidity early
questions.why: A liquidity lock proves devs committed their LP for a period of time — they physically can't rug before the lock expires.

questions.q: Which is a major red flag on a new token?
questions.answer: Dev wallet holds 40% of supply
questions.why: Concentrated dev wallet = concentrated dump risk. If they hold 40%, one sell can collapse the price.

questions.q: A project DMs you saying you won a giveaway and need to connect your wallet to claim. What do you do?
questions.answer: Ignore and report — it's a scam
questions.why: Unsolicited DMs asking you to connect your wallet are almost always phishing scams. Legitimate projects don't give away tokens through cold DMs.

questions.q: What is social engineering in crypto?
questions.answer: Psychologically manipulating people to gain trust before scamming them
questions.why: Social engineering is when scammers build fake relationships or urgency to trick you into giving up access to your wallet or funds.

lessons.title: Volatility & Weak Hands
lessons.intro: Crypto moves fast. 50% drops in hours. 10x runs overnight. Money is lost both ways: panic-selling a good project at the bottom, and refusing to sell a project that's actually broken. The skill is telling those two apart.

concepts.def: The rate at which a price moves up or down. High vol = big swings both ways.
Traders who sell at the first sign of red, usually locking in losses at the worst moment.
Holding through extreme volatility without panic selling.
A pre-set price where you automatically sell to limit downside. Discipline over emotion.
Buying fixed amounts at regular intervals regardless of price. Reduces timing risk.

questions.q: What do weak hands do during a price dip?
questions.answer: Panic sell, locking in losses
questions.why: Weak hands react emotionally — they sell a sound project the moment it dips, often right before recovery. The discipline is holding through volatility when nothing has actually changed about the project.

questions.q: What is a stop loss?
questions.answer: A pre-set automatic sell to limit downside
questions.why: A stop loss removes emotion from the equation. You pre-decide your exit — the market doesn't get to decide for you.

questions.q: High volatility means:
questions.answer: Large price swings in both directions
questions.why: Volatility is neutral — it means big moves happen. That means big gains AND big losses are both possible.

questions.q: What is Dollar Cost Averaging (DCA)?
questions.answer: Buying fixed amounts at regular intervals regardless of price
questions.why: DCA removes the pressure of timing the market. You buy $50 every week whether price is up or down — over time it averages out your entry price.

questions.q: A token drops 60% in a day. A disciplined trader would:
questions.answer: Find out WHY it dropped before doing anything
questions.why: A 60% drop is information. It could be market-wide noise — or a hack, a vesting unlock, or a whale heading for the exit. A disciplined trader finds out the cause first. Only once you know WHY can you decide whether to buy, hold, or cut it.

lessons.title: Wallets & Keys
lessons.intro: Your wallet doesn't hold tokens — the blockchain does. Your wallet holds the KEYS that prove ownership. Lose the keys, lose everything. Forever.

concepts.def: A secret string that gives full control over your wallet. Never share it. Ever.
12-24 words that regenerate your private key. Write it on paper. Never digitally.
An exchange holds your keys. Convenient but risky — 'not your keys, not your coins.'
You hold your own keys. Full control. Full responsibility. Phantom, Backpack, etc.
A physical device that stores your private key offline. Most secure option for large holdings.

questions.q: What does 'not your keys, not your coins' mean?
questions.answer: If an exchange holds your keys, they control your funds
questions.why: When a CEX holds your keys, they actually control your funds. If they go bankrupt or freeze withdrawals — you have no recourse.

questions.q: Where should you store your seed phrase?
questions.answer: Written on paper, stored offline
questions.why: Seed phrases stored digitally can be hacked. Paper doesn't get hacked. Store it offline, somewhere safe.

questions.q: What is a non-custodial wallet?
questions.answer: A wallet where you control your own private keys
questions.why: Non-custodial means YOU hold the keys. Phantom, Backpack, and Solflare are non-custodial Solana wallets.

questions.q: Why is a hardware wallet more secure than a software wallet?
questions.answer: It stores your private key offline, away from internet threats
questions.why: Hardware wallets keep your private key on a physical device that never touches the internet. Even if your computer is hacked, your keys are safe.

questions.q: Someone online says they can recover your lost crypto if you give them your seed phrase. What do you do?
questions.answer: Never share your seed phrase with anyone, ever
questions.why: Your seed phrase gives complete control of your wallet. Anyone who asks for it is trying to steal your funds. No legitimate service ever needs your seed phrase.

lessons.title: Slippage & MEV
lessons.intro: Every time you swap on a DEX, bots are watching. They can see your trade and rush to get their own transaction ordered right in front of it — buying first to push the price up, so you buy higher, then selling into you. It's called a sandwich attack. Knowing this changes how you trade.

concepts.def: The difference between the price you expect and the price you actually get.
Maximal Extractable Value — profit bots extract by reordering transactions within a block.
A bot buys before your trade (raising price), lets you buy higher, then sells for profit.
The max % price change you'll accept. Set too high = bot target. Too low = failed trade.
A bot sees your pending transaction and executes the same trade first to profit from your price impact.

questions.q: What is a sandwich attack?
questions.answer: A bot buys before and sells after your trade to profit at your expense
questions.why: Sandwich bots front-run your swap, then back-run it. You pay more, they profit. Setting tight slippage is your defense.

questions.q: What does setting a LOW slippage tolerance do?
questions.answer: Protects you from sandwich attacks but may cause failed transactions
questions.why: Low slippage = trade only executes if price stays close to what you expect. Bots can't profitably sandwich you, but you risk the trade failing.

questions.q: What does MEV stand for?
questions.answer: Maximal Extractable Value
questions.why: MEV is profit extracted by validators or bots who control transaction ordering.

questions.q: What is front-running?
questions.answer: A bot executing the same trade as you but before your transaction confirms
questions.why: Front-running bots watch for large pending trades and rush to get their own transaction ordered first, profiting from the price impact your trade will cause. On Ethereum they do this via the public mempool; Solana has no public mempool, so bots race transaction ordering at the validator instead.

questions.q: On Solana, MEV is:
questions.answer: Very real — sandwich bots pay validators for ordering instead of watching a public mempool
questions.why: Solana has no public mempool, so bots cannot watch pending trades the Ethereum way — but they pay validators for transaction ordering (Jito bundles), and sandwich attacks on Jupiter and Raydium routes are common, especially during launches. Speed does not remove MEV. Tight slippage is your defence.

lessons.title: Tokenomics
lessons.intro: Tokenomics is the economics of a token — supply, distribution, vesting, and inflation. A token with bad tokenomics will dump no matter how good the project is.

concepts.def: The max number of tokens that will ever exist.
How many tokens are actually tradeable right now.
A lock-up period for team/investor tokens. Watch unlock dates.
How tokens are split between team, investors, community, treasury.
Permanently removing tokens from circulation to reduce supply over time.

questions.q: Why does vesting schedule matter to traders?
questions.answer: It shows when locked team/investor tokens unlock and can be sold
questions.why: When a vesting cliff hits, millions of insider tokens unlock. If team or VCs sell, price can crash hard.

questions.q: A token has 1 trillion total supply and costs $0.001. Is it cheap?
questions.answer: No — supply determines real value, not price per token
questions.why: 1 trillion tokens × $0.001 = a $1B market cap. A sub-penny price tells you nothing on its own — supply is what makes a project big or small.

questions.q: What is circulating supply?
questions.answer: Tokens currently tradeable in the market
questions.why: Circulating supply is what's actually on the market. Market cap = price × circulating supply.

questions.q: What does a burn mechanism do?
questions.answer: Permanently removes tokens from circulation reducing supply
questions.why: Burning tokens reduces supply over time. If demand stays the same and supply decreases, price pressure is upward. A burn on a token nobody wants changes nothing — demand still has to be there.

questions.q: A token has 5% team allocation with a 4-year vesting schedule. Is this good or bad?
questions.answer: Good — low alloc with long vesting
questions.why: Low team allocation with long vesting is a green flag. It means the team can't dump on holders early and is incentivized to build long-term value.

questions.q: What happens to price when a large vesting unlock occurs?
questions.answer: Price often drops as insiders sell their newly unlocked tokens
questions.why: Vesting unlocks create sell pressure. Even if markets partially price it in, the actual unlock often causes a price dip as insiders take profits.

lessons.title: Market Cap vs Price
lessons.intro: The biggest beginner mistake in crypto: thinking a $0.001 token is cheaper than $50,000 BTC. Price per token means nothing. Market cap is everything.

concepts.def: Price × Circulating Supply. The real size of a project.
Fully Diluted Valuation — Price × the full supply, counting every token that will ever exist (including locked and not-yet-released ones).
Meaningless without supply context.
Low cap (<$10M) = more upside, more risk. Large cap (>$1B) = more stable, harder to 10x.
A $10M market cap token with $50K liquidity can't absorb large buys without massive price impact.

questions.q: Token A: $0.001 price, 1 trillion supply. Token B: $100 price, 100,000 supply. Which has the higher market cap?
questions.answer: Token A — $1B market cap vs Token B's $10M
questions.why: Token A: $0.001 × 1T = $1B. Token B: $100 × 100K = $10M. Price per token is meaningless.

questions.q: What does FDV tell you?
questions.answer: What market cap would be if all tokens were in circulation
questions.why: FDV uses total supply including locked tokens. High FDV vs market cap = lots of potential sell pressure ahead.

questions.q: For a $1M investment to 100x, what must happen?
questions.answer: The market cap must also 100x
questions.why: Your return is tied to market cap growth. A project at $500M market cap needs $50B to 100x — much harder.

questions.q: A token has a $1M market cap but only $10K in liquidity. What does this mean?
questions.answer: Even a small buy will cause massive price impact — very risky
questions.why: Low liquidity means your buy moves the price dramatically — and selling is even harder. You could buy in easily but be trapped when trying to exit.

questions.q: Why is FDV often higher than market cap?
questions.answer: Because many tokens are locked, vesting, or not yet released
questions.why: FDV accounts for ALL tokens that will ever exist. Locked team tokens, vesting allocations, and unreleased supply all count toward FDV but not market cap.

questions.q: A project has $100M market cap and $1B FDV. What does this signal?
questions.answer: 90% of tokens are still locked — massive future sell pressure likely
questions.why: When FDV is 10x market cap, it means 90% of tokens haven't hit the market yet. As they unlock, sustained sell pressure can suppress price for years.

lessons.title: DEX vs CEX
lessons.intro: Two ways to trade crypto. CEX is the on-ramp — easy, regulated, ID required. DEX is the frontier — permissionless, self-custody, always open.

concepts.def: Centralized Exchange (Coinbase, Binance). Requires ID. Holds your keys. Regulated.
Decentralized Exchange (Jupiter, Raydium). No ID. You keep your keys. No central operator who can freeze you out.
Know Your Customer — identity verification required by CEXs.
Matches buyers and sellers at specific prices. Standard on CEXs; a few on-chain Solana DEXs (OpenBook, Phoenix) use one too.
You control your own keys. No third party can freeze or seize your funds.

questions.q: What does a CEX require that a DEX does not?
questions.answer: Identity verification (KYC)
questions.why: CEXs are regulated businesses — they require ID. DEXs are permissionless smart contracts. No ID, no account.

questions.q: What is slippage on a DEX?
questions.answer: The difference between expected and actual trade price
questions.why: Low liquidity = high slippage. For small-cap tokens, even a modest trade can move the price significantly.

questions.q: Which is always available 24/7 with no downtime?
questions.answer: DEX — it's a smart contract on the blockchain
questions.why: The DEX smart contract has no maintenance windows and no company that can freeze your account — it runs as long as the blockchain does. Two honest caveats: the website front-end you use to reach it can still go down or be hacked, and the blockchain itself can have outages (Solana has had them). 'Decentralized' is not the same as 'never fails.'

questions.q: What is the biggest risk of keeping funds on a CEX?
questions.answer: The CEX can freeze withdrawals, get hacked, or go bankrupt
questions.why: FTX, Celsius, and many others showed the risk — when a CEX fails, user funds can disappear overnight. Not your keys, not your coins.

questions.q: What does self-custody mean?
questions.answer: Controlling your own private keys with no third party involvement
questions.why: Self-custody means you hold your own keys. No exchange, no bank, no government can freeze or seize your funds without physical access to your device.

lessons.title: On-Chain Analysis
lessons.intro: Every transaction on Solana is public and permanent. On-chain analysis means reading this data to understand who is buying, who is selling, where the smart money is going, and whether a project is healthy or dying. This is the edge most retail traders never develop.

concepts.def: Monitoring specific wallet addresses to see when whales buy, sell, or move tokens.
Every swap, transfer, and interaction a wallet has ever made — all public on-chain.
Block explorers that let you read Solana transaction data in human-readable form.
A wallet holding a large amount of a token. When whales move, price often follows.
Wallets consistently making profitable trades — often early VCs, insiders, or skilled traders.

questions.q: What can on-chain analysis reveal that price charts cannot?
questions.answer: Who is actually buying and selling, and in what size
questions.why: Price charts show the result of trading activity. On-chain data shows who is doing it — whether whales are accumulating, insiders are dumping, or smart money is entering.

questions.q: What is a block explorer?
questions.answer: A website that lets you read all blockchain transaction data
questions.why: Solscan and Solana Explorer let you look up any wallet address, transaction, or token on Solana. Everything is public — no account needed.

questions.q: A whale wallet you track just bought $500K of a token you've never heard of. What should you do?
questions.answer: Research the token and understand why before making any decision
questions.why: Whale activity is a signal worth investigating — but not a guaranteed buy signal. Research what the token is first. Whales can also be wrong, or already planning to exit.

questions.q: What does it mean when multiple new wallets buy a token right before a major price spike?
questions.answer: Possible insider trading or coordinated buying
questions.why: When fresh wallets with no history suddenly appear right before a pump, it often suggests insider knowledge or coordinated activity. This is a yellow flag worth noting.

questions.q: On Solana, all transactions are:
questions.answer: Public and permanently visible to anyone
questions.why: The blockchain is a public ledger. Every transaction you've ever made is permanently visible to anyone with a block explorer. There is no privacy on-chain without specific privacy tools.

questions.q: What is 'smart money' in crypto?
questions.answer: Wallets that consistently make profitable early trades
questions.why: Smart money wallets consistently buy early and exit before crashes. Tracking them doesn't guarantee copying their success — they have information advantages you don't — but it's valuable signal.

questions.q: A token's top 10 wallets hold 80% of supply. Is this a red flag?
questions.answer: Yes — extreme concentration means a few wallets can crash the price at will
questions.why: Highly concentrated supply is a major risk. If the top 10 holders decide to sell simultaneously, no amount of buying pressure can stop the crash. Always check token distribution.

lessons.title: Staking & Yield Farming
lessons.intro: Staking and yield farming let your crypto work for you while you hold. But high APY comes with real risks that most beginners ignore. Understanding what you're actually earning — and what you're risking — is the difference between growing wealth and losing it.

concepts.def: Locking tokens to support a network or protocol in exchange for rewards.
Annual Percentage Yield — the yearly return on your staked or farmed assets.
Providing liquidity to DeFi protocols in exchange for token rewards, often at high APY.
When staking rewards are paid by minting new tokens — diluting all existing holders.
Time you must wait before unstaking. You can't sell during this period.

questions.q: What does staking mean?
questions.answer: Locking tokens to support a network in exchange for rewards
questions.why: Staking involves locking your tokens in a protocol — either to validate transactions (proof of stake) or to earn protocol rewards. In return you receive staking rewards.

questions.q: A protocol offers 500% APY. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.answer: The rewards are paid in new tokens being minted — heavily inflationary
questions.why: Extremely high APY is almost always funded by token inflation. The protocol mints new tokens to pay you — but this dilutes the token's value. Your 500% APY might be worth very little if the token crashes.

questions.q: What is impermanent loss in yield farming?
questions.answer: Value loss compared to just holding when token prices diverge in an LP
questions.why: When you provide liquidity and token prices diverge, the AMM rebalances your position. You end up with less of the token that went up. This loss is 'impermanent' but can become permanent if you exit.

questions.q: What is a lock-up period?
questions.answer: The time you must wait before you can unstake and access your tokens
questions.why: Many staking protocols require you to lock your tokens for days, weeks, or months. During a crash, you cannot sell — this is a critical risk to understand before staking.

questions.q: What does APY stand for?
questions.answer: Annual Percentage Yield
questions.why: APY is Annual Percentage Yield — your projected return over a full year including compounding. Compare this to APR (Annual Percentage Rate) which doesn't include compounding.

questions.q: You stake a token earning 100% APY. The token loses 80% of its value over the year. What happened?
questions.answer: You lost money — token price decline exceeded your staking rewards
questions.why: APY is paid in the token you're earning. Start with $100, earn 100% APY → you hold 2× the tokens. But the token's price fell 80%: twice the tokens at one-fifth the price = $40. You're down 60%, despite the '100% APY.' Always weigh token price risk against the headline yield.

questions.q: What is the safest type of yield in DeFi?
questions.answer: Yield from real protocol fees (not token emissions)
questions.why: Real yield — paid from actual protocol fee revenue rather than token inflation — is the most sustainable. It's usually lower APY but backed by real economic activity, not just token printing.

lessons.title: How Bags.fm Works
lessons.intro: Bags.fm is a Solana token launchpad where creators earn 1% of all trading volume forever. Understanding how it works — from launch to graduation to fee claiming — gives you an edge when evaluating any Bags.fm token.

concepts.def: The initial launch mechanism. Price increases as more tokens are bought along a curve.
When a token raises enough SOL on the bonding curve to migrate to a full Meteora DAMM V2 liquidity pool.
1% of all trading volume goes to the token creator — forever, whether they're active or not.
A referral code that earns a % of platform fees when users trade through your link.
The graduated liquidity pool — deeper liquidity, tighter spreads, more professional trading environment.

questions.q: What is the DBC phase on Bags.fm?
questions.answer: The initial bonding curve launch phase where price rises with each buy
questions.why: DBC stands for Dynamic Bonding Curve. When a token launches on Bags.fm, it starts on a bonding curve — each buy raises the price slightly. Once enough SOL is raised, it graduates to a full liquidity pool.

questions.q: What does graduation mean on Bags.fm?
questions.answer: The token migrates from bonding curve to a full Meteora liquidity pool
questions.why: Graduation is a milestone — it means the token raised enough initial liquidity to move to Meteora DAMM V2, a professional AMM pool. Graduated tokens have deeper liquidity and more stable trading.

questions.q: How much do Bags.fm creators earn from trading volume?
questions.why: Creators earn 1% of all trading volume on their token — forever. This means the more people trade your token, the more you earn, even if you never touch the project again.

questions.q: What is a partner ref code on Bags.fm?
questions.answer: A referral code that earns a % of platform fees
questions.why: A partner ref code earns a share of platform fees when other people's tokens are launched or traded through your link — it's a referral mechanism, separate from the fees a token earns on its own trading.

questions.q: What is Meteora DAMM V2?
questions.answer: A graduated liquidity pool providing deeper, more stable trading
questions.why: Meteora DAMM V2 is where Bags.fm tokens go after graduation. It is Meteora's dynamic AMM — a constant-product style pool with configurable, dynamic fees (not concentrated liquidity; that is Meteora's DLMM). It gives the token a real two-sided pool with deeper liquidity and better trading conditions than the bonding curve.

questions.q: If a Bags.fm token never graduates, what happens?
questions.answer: It stays on the bonding curve indefinitely
questions.why: Not every Bags.fm token graduates. If a token doesn't attract enough buying pressure to fill the bonding curve, it stays there indefinitely. Many tokens fail at this stage — research is critical.

questions.q: Where does a Bags.fm token's own project revenue actually come from?
questions.answer: The creator fee — a cut of every trade of that token
questions.why: A token's project revenue is the creator fee — roughly 1% of every trade of that token. A partner ref code is a separate thing that earns from OTHER projects routed through it, not the token's own trades. CLKN reinvests 100% of its creator fee back into buying CLKN.

lessons.title: Memecoins & Culture
lessons.intro: Memecoins are the most volatile, most dangerous, and most exciting corner of crypto. They have no utility — their value is entirely driven by community, narrative, and timing. Understanding how they work is how you survive them.

concepts.def: A token with no inherent utility — value is driven purely by community, narrative, and speculation.
The story or theme driving a memecoin's momentum. Dog coins, political figures, viral memes.
The single most important factor in a memecoin's success. A strong community creates buying pressure and holds through dips.
Coordinated buying to raise price followed by coordinated selling — leaving late buyers holding worthless bags.
High-risk, high-reward trading strategy focused on early memecoin entries with small position sizes.

questions.q: What gives a memecoin its value?
questions.answer: Community belief, narrative, and speculation
questions.why: Memecoins have no fundamental value — no product, no revenue, no utility. Their value is entirely narrative-driven. The meme, the community, and the timing determine everything.

questions.q: What is the most important factor in a memecoin's long-term survival?
questions.answer: A strong, engaged community that believes in the narrative
questions.why: Memecoins that survive are held together by community. When the community believes and holds through dips, the token has a chance. When community leaves, it's over — no fundamentals to fall back on.

questions.q: What is a pump and dump scheme?
questions.answer: Coordinated buying to inflate price, then coordinated selling
questions.why: Pump and dump groups coordinate buying to create artificial price spikes, then exit simultaneously. Late buyers — usually retail — are left holding worthless tokens. This is illegal in traditional markets but common in crypto.

questions.q: What does degen trading mean?
questions.answer: High-risk early entries into speculative tokens with small position sizes
questions.why: Degen (degenerate) trading is high-risk speculation — usually early entries into memecoins or new launches. Experienced degens use small position sizes, take profits early, and accept that most bets will fail.

questions.q: You find a brand new memecoin at a $10K market cap with a funny meme. What is the correct risk management approach?
questions.answer: Only invest what you can completely afford to lose — treat it like a lottery ticket
questions.why: Ultra small cap memecoins are essentially lottery tickets. The upside can be enormous but the probability of failure is very high. Only ever invest what you can afford to completely lose — because you probably will.

questions.q: What is narrative in memecoin culture?
questions.answer: The story or theme driving community excitement and buying pressure
questions.why: Narrative is everything in memecoin culture. 'Dog with hat', political figures, AI themes, animal coins — when a narrative captures the zeitgeist, it drives viral spread and buying pressure. Without narrative, there's nothing.

questions.q: CLKN is a memecoin built on Bags.fm. What makes it different from a typical memecoin?
questions.answer: It has a real education platform behind it
questions.why: CLKN pairs the token with an actual utility layer — the School of Crypto Hard Knocks — and reinvests its creator fee back into the token. That doesn't make it safe: like any memecoin it can still go to zero. But a token doing real work is rarer than one that isn't.

lessons.title: Seed Phrase Survival
lessons.intro: Your seed phrase is not a password. A password can be reset by someone who can prove who you are. A seed phrase cannot. It is the wallet itself, written down — anyone holding those words owns everything in it, from anywhere, forever, and there is nobody to appeal to. Far more crypto has been lost to bad backups than to hackers.

concepts.def: 12 or 24 words in a fixed order that regenerate every key in your wallet. Order matters. There is no 'forgot my phrase' link, and no support desk that can help.
A screenshot, a notes app, a photo, a password manager, a cloud backup, a chat to yourself. All of these have drained real people. Your phone quietly uploads your photos — that is the point of it.
Paper burns, floods, fades and gets thrown out by someone tidying up. Stamped steel survives a house fire. If losing it would genuinely hurt, use metal.

An optional extra word that turns your seed into a completely DIFFERENT wallet. Real protection if someone finds your words — and permanent loss if you forget it, because the seed alone will not open it.
Restoring your backup into a fresh wallet BEFORE it holds real money. An untested backup is a guess, and people discover the guess was wrong at the worst possible moment.
Cutting your 24 words into two halves of 12 is NOT half the risk — each half shrinks the guessing problem enormously. Proper splitting schemes exist precisely because the obvious approach is weak.

questions.q: Which of these is a safe place for a seed phrase?
questions.answer: Written or stamped on something physical, stored offline
questions.why: Anything on a device that touches the internet can be reached — by malware, by a cloud breach, or by someone who picks up your unlocked phone. Photos are the worst of these because phones upload them automatically. Offline and physical is the baseline.

questions.q: What does adding a passphrase — the optional '25th word' — actually do?
questions.answer: Creates an entirely different wallet that the seed alone will not open
questions.why: The passphrase combines with your seed to derive a different wallet. Someone who steals your 24 words gets an empty wallet. But forget the passphrase and your funds are unreachable even though you still have every word — this protection cuts both ways.

questions.q: You split your 24 words into two halves and store them in two locations. How much harder is your wallet to crack?
questions.answer: Far less than you would expect — each half massively narrows the search
questions.why: It feels like halving the risk and it isn't. Finding 12 of 24 words leaves a vastly smaller problem than starting from nothing, and you have now doubled the number of places you can permanently lose half your backup. Splitting done properly needs a scheme designed for it, not scissors.

questions.q: Why restore your backup into a fresh wallet before funding it?
questions.answer: It proves the backup actually works while a mistake is still cheap
questions.why: A word written down wrong, a missing word, an unreadable letter, the wrong order — none of these announce themselves. You find out when you try to restore, and by then the mistake costs whatever the wallet holds. Test it while it holds nothing.

questions.q: Wallet support messages you: they need your seed phrase to fix a failed transaction. What is happening?
questions.answer: It is a theft attempt. No legitimate service ever needs your seed phrase
questions.why: There is no exception to this and there never will be. No wallet, no exchange, no support agent, no airdrop, no 'validation' page needs your seed phrase for any reason. The request itself is the entire scam — everything around it is decoration.

lessons.title: If Something Happens To You
lessons.intro: A bank has a process for death. Paperwork, a death certificate, a next of kin, someone to call. A blockchain has none of that. If nobody living can reach your seed phrase, those coins do not go to your family — they stop existing for everyone, permanently. A large share of all lost crypto was never stolen. It was simply never passed on.

concepts.def: There is no account to close, no branch to visit, no form to file. A wallet nobody can open is not frozen or held in trust — it is gone, and nobody on earth can change that.

In many countries a will becomes a public record once it goes through probate. Writing your seed phrase into your will can publish it to anyone who asks for a copy. Never put the words themselves in a will.
A sealed document that explains WHAT exists and WHERE to find it — which wallets, which devices, who to ask for help — without containing the secret itself. The map, kept separately from the key.
A wallet that needs, say, 2 of 3 keys to move anything. A partner and a lawyer together can act; neither alone can steal, and neither alone losing a key is fatal.

A service that releases your secrets if you stop checking in. Convenient, and also a single point of failure someone can attack, and a thing that fires by accident when you are on holiday with no signal.

Can the person you chose actually do it — find the words, install the wallet, restore it? Walk them through it while you are alive. Almost nobody does this, and it is the step that decides whether any of the rest worked.

questions.q: You die tomorrow and nobody can reach your seed phrase. What happens to your crypto?
questions.answer: It stays in the wallet forever and nobody can ever move it
questions.why: The coins remain visible on-chain for anyone to look at, and unreachable by everyone for the rest of time. There is no authority holding a spare key, because the entire design is that no such authority exists. This is the trade you accepted when you took custody.

questions.q: Why is writing your seed phrase into your will a bad idea?
questions.answer: A will often becomes a public record in probate, exposing the phrase
questions.why: In many jurisdictions a probated will becomes a public document that anyone can request. Your will should point to where the phrase is kept and who can help — it should never contain the words. Talk to an estate professional where you live about how to do this properly.

questions.q: What is a letter of instruction meant to contain?
questions.answer: What exists and where to find it, without the secret itself
questions.why: It is the map, not the key. Which wallets exist, which device or safe holds the backup, who understands crypto well enough to help, and what your wishes are. Kept somewhere your family will actually look, and separate from the backup itself.

questions.q: What does a 2-of-3 multisig give an inheritance plan that a single seed phrase cannot?
questions.answer: Recovery by trusted people together, with no one person able to steal
questions.why: Splitting authority means your partner and your lawyer can act together, but neither can act alone — and losing one key does not end the story. It removes both failure modes of a single phrase: one person who can steal everything, or one lost backup that ends everything.

questions.q: Which step do people most often skip, and most regret skipping?
questions.answer: Actually telling someone the crypto exists and checking they could reach it
questions.why: A perfect backup in a safe nobody knows about is the same as no backup. The plan has to survive contact with a grieving family who may not know crypto exists at all. Tell someone it exists, tell them where the instructions are, and walk them through a restore while you still can.

lessons.title: Read a Payout Receipt
lessons.intro: A payout receipt is not a promise — it's a record of money that already moved, with the numbers behind it published so nobody has to take your word, our word, or the project's word for it. A real one names which rules paid it, why the wallet qualified, what its term earned, and the exact transaction that sent it. If a receipt's own math does not add up to the number it claims to pay, that mismatch is the whole story — and the point of publishing everything is that a stranger can find it, not just us.

concepts.def: Every payout runs under a published program version — the exact term rules in force at the time. Its hash is a fingerprint of those rules: change one number in the terms and the hash changes too. A receipt names the version that paid it, so you check the rules that actually applied, not whatever the page shows today.

Before anything accrues, the program checks whether a lock actually qualifies — right token, non-cancelable, term long enough. Each check leaves a reason code behind it, so 'why didn't this hour pay me' has a checkable answer instead of a shrug.

How long you committed decides your rate: 1x at the minimum term, rising toward the top rate at the maximum. That multiplier is fixed by the published rule the day you locked — not chosen after the fact, and not the day you got paid.

Every hour, that hour's pool splits across everyone who qualified — your share is your locked amount times your term, divided by everyone else's. It moves: down when more people lock, up when locks end. Nobody promised a fixed number, because the pool is shared, not fixed.

The actual transaction that sent the tokens — look it up on any explorer yourself. A real receipt separates what was OWED for a period from what was actually APPLIED to it; a partial payment's difference carries forward as a remainder, never quietly written off as excess.

The program version, the accrual periods, and the ledger behind a receipt are all published. A script on your own machine — or a page in your own browser — can re-run that arithmetic from those published inputs and land on the same number, offline, without asking anyone to be trusted.

questions.q: You re-run a receipt's published inputs yourself and get a different total than the receipt claims. What does that mismatch mean?
questions.answer: A real finding: something in the published inputs or the receipt does not reconcile, and it should be reported, not assumed correct
questions.why: A mismatch is a genuine signal, not noise. It means what actually shipped doesn't reconcile with the inputs published for it — a bug, a bad input, or worse. The entire point of publishing the raw materials is that a stranger can catch this instead of taking the number on faith.

questions.q: A program page says its receipts are "reproducible from published inputs." What does that specific claim mean?
questions.answer: Anyone can run the same public numbers through the same public method and land on the same answer, without trusting anyone's word for it
questions.why: "Reproducible" is a narrower, more honest claim than "verified." It means the inputs and the method are both public, so you can run it yourself instead of trusting someone's say-so. It only upgrades to "independently committed" once something outside the project — like an on-chain memo — has actually observed the commitment. That is a stronger, later claim, never assumed in advance.

questions.q: A receipt shows a reason code next to an hour that earned nothing. What is a reason code actually telling you?
questions.answer: Which specific published eligibility rule that hour's check failed or passed — an audit trail, not a guess
questions.why: Every eligibility check the program runs — right token, non-cancelable, term met — leaves a code behind its outcome. That turns "why didn't this hour pay me" into an answer you can check against the published rule yourself, not a mystery someone has to explain to you.

questions.q: What does a program version's hash actually commit to?
questions.answer: The exact term rules in force when your accrual ran — edit the terms even slightly and the hash changes too
questions.why: The hash fingerprints the rules themselves — the term range, the multiplier curve, everything a program version fixes. It has nothing to do with balances or prices. Naming a receipt's version and hash lets you check the rules that actually applied to it, not the ones a page happens to show today.

questions.q: You lock tokens into a rewards program. Is locking the same thing as selling them?
questions.answer: No — a lock immobilizes tokens for a set time under published terms; nothing is sold, and you own them the whole time
questions.why: A lock is a public promise not to move tokens for a period — an on-chain escrow you can go open and inspect yourself. It is not a transfer of ownership or a swap for something else. You remain the owner the entire time; you've only committed not to touch them until the date, which is exactly what makes the promise checkable in the first place.

lessons.title: The Deposit You Didn't Know You Made
lessons.intro: Open a token account and your wallet balance drops by a fraction of a SOL, before you've bought anything. That's not a fee. It's a rent-exempt deposit — Solana requires it so the account's data stays paid for, and it comes back to you when you're done with the account. Nobody explains this the first time it happens, so it feels like money vanishing into the network. It never left. It's still yours.

concepts.def: A refundable amount of SOL locked when an account is created — not a fee, not spent. It's sized to the account's data, and it's returned to you when the account is closed.
What actually gets priced: a standard SPL token account holds 165 bytes of data, plus a fixed 128-byte account-overhead allowance Solana also charges rent on — 293 billable bytes in total.

The network upgrade cutting the per-byte rate in stages — live on mainnet since Sep 3, 2026, with the remaining steps expected around November 2026 — heading toward roughly a 90% cut from the original rate.
Returns the account's ENTIRE current rent-exempt deposit to its owner. It only makes sense once you're actually finished holding that token — you'd need to pay the deposit again to reopen it.

A newer instruction that pulls out only the surplus above today's required minimum, without closing the account or touching your token balance. The account owner signs it, and it can never take the account below the current minimum.

A predictable wave of fake claim sites cashing in on real news about the rent cut. Nobody needs your seed phrase, a token delegate approval, or a SOL 'unlock fee' to hand back a deposit that was always yours.

questions.q: You open a fresh token account and a small amount of SOL leaves your wallet immediately, before any trade happens. What is that SOL?
questions.answer: A refundable rent-exempt deposit sized to the account's data
questions.why: It's a rent-exempt deposit, not a fee — the network requires it so the account's data stays paid for. It's sized to the account, and it's still yours: you get it back when you close the account.

questions.q: A standard SPL token account holds 165 bytes of data. Why is the rent-exempt deposit actually priced on 293 bytes?
questions.answer: Solana also charges rent on a fixed 128-byte account-overhead allowance, on top of the 165 bytes of data
questions.why: 165 bytes of token-account data plus a fixed 128-byte account-overhead allowance Solana also charges rent on equals 293 billable bytes — the number the deposit is actually calculated against.

questions.q: Solana is cutting the rent-exempt rate in stages. A headline says 'hundreds of thousands of SOL unlocked.' What is that number actually counting?
questions.answer: The whole network's accounts added together — your own share is a fraction of a cent
questions.why: Nothing new is being created. The rate drop applies across every token account on the network, and adding all of that up produces a big-sounding total — your own share of it is currently a fraction of a cent per account.

questions.q: You're completely done with a token and will never hold it again. What does closing that account return to you?
questions.answer: The account's entire current rent-exempt deposit
questions.why: Closing an account you're finished with returns the WHOLE rent-exempt deposit it's currently holding — worth more per account than only pulling out the surplus.

questions.q: You still hold a token and want the account to stay open, but rates have dropped since you opened it. What does WithdrawExcessLamports actually do?
questions.answer: Moves out only the surplus above today's required minimum, without closing the account or touching your token balance
questions.why: It's a narrower tool than closing an account: it withdraws only the surplus above the current minimum, leaves the account open, never touches your token balance, and can never take the account below what's currently required. The account owner has to sign it.

questions.q: A site tells you to sign a message and approve a token delegate to 'claim your reduced-rent refund.' What is actually happening?
questions.answer: This is the exact scam the rent cut invites — nobody needs your seed phrase, a delegate approval, or an 'unlock fee' to return a deposit that was already yours
questions.why: This is the predictable next wave — the same way every past airdrop bred a wave of fake claim pages. Real amounts today are fractions of a cent per account. Anything asking for a delegate, a seed phrase, or SOL up front to 'unlock' your own money is lying. Close the tab.

courses.blurb: Brand new? Start here — wallets, tokens, on-ramps, what a DEX even is, staying safe.

lessons.title: What is a Wallet?
lessons.intro: In crypto, a wallet doesn't hold money — it holds KEYS. Your wallet is basically a password manager for your crypto. There are two keys you need to know about.

concepts.def: Like your home address — you can share it with anyone so they can send you crypto. It's safe to show.
Like the key to your front door. NEVER share this with anyone. Whoever has it owns your crypto.
A wallet where YOU control the keys. Examples: Phantom, MetaMask. You are your own bank.
A wallet controlled by a company (like a Coinbase exchange account). They hold your keys — if they go down, you could lose access.

questions.q: Your public key is like your home address — safe to share so people can send you crypto.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: Correct! Your public key is safe to share. It's how others send crypto to you. Never confuse it with your private key or seed phrase.

questions.q: You should share your seed phrase with customer support if they ask for it.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: NEVER share your seed phrase with anyone — ever. Legitimate support teams will never ask for it. Anyone asking is trying to steal your crypto.

questions.q: With a non-custodial wallet, who controls your crypto?
questions.answer: You do
questions.why: Non-custodial means YOU hold the keys. No company can freeze or take your funds. With great power comes great responsibility — back up your seed phrase!

lessons.title: What is a Token?
lessons.intro: You've probably heard 'coin' and 'token' used interchangeably — but they're different. Understanding this helps you know what you're actually buying.

concepts.def: A native cryptocurrency that powers its own blockchain. Examples: SOL (Solana), ETH (Ethereum), BTC (Bitcoin).
A crypto asset built ON TOP of an existing blockchain. CLKN is a token built on Solana. Tokens don't have their own blockchain.
The unique ID of a token on Solana — like a social security number for the token. Used to identify the exact token you're buying.
The total number of tokens that exist. A fixed supply means no more can ever be created.

questions.q: SOL is a token built on the Ethereum blockchain.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: SOL is actually the native coin of the Solana blockchain — not Ethereum. Tokens are built ON a blockchain, while coins ARE the blockchain's currency.

questions.q: What is CLKN?
questions.answer: A token built on Solana
questions.why: CLKN is a Solana token — it lives on the Solana blockchain and uses SOL for transactions. It doesn't have its own blockchain.

questions.q: Why does a token's mint address matter?
questions.answer: It uniquely identifies the exact token so you don't buy a fake copy
questions.why: Scammers create fake tokens with similar names. The mint address is the only guaranteed way to confirm you have the right token. Always verify!

lessons.title: On-Ramps & Off-Ramps
lessons.intro: Before you can do anything in crypto you have to get some — and one day you'll want to cash some out. The bridge between regular money and crypto is called a ramp. Knowing how ramps work is genuinely step one.

concepts.def: Any service that turns government money — dollars, euros — into crypto. It's your way in: connect a bank account or card, buy crypto, and it lands in a wallet.
The reverse trip — turning crypto back into regular money in your bank. You sell crypto for cash and withdraw it. Always understand your exit before you need it.

The most common ramp. Companies like Coinbase, Kraken, and Binance let you buy crypto with a bank transfer or card — then you can withdraw it to your own wallet. A CEX works as both an on-ramp and an off-ramp.

By law, ramps must verify your identity — KYC, 'Know Your Customer' — so expect to upload a photo ID. Ramps also charge fees; instant card-buy services like MoonPay are fast but cost more. Always check the fee before you confirm.

questions.q: An on-ramp is any service that turns regular money, like dollars, into crypto.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: Correct. An on-ramp is your entry point — connect a bank or card, buy crypto, and it arrives in your wallet. The off-ramp is the same trip in reverse, back to cash.

questions.q: You can buy crypto on a major exchange like Coinbase without ever verifying your identity.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. By law, on-ramps must do KYC — Know Your Customer — so expect to upload a photo ID. Any 'exchange' that skips identity checks entirely is a red flag.

questions.q: Why should you understand off-ramps before you put any money in?
questions.answer: So you know exactly how to cash out — the fees, the wait, the steps — before you ever need to
questions.why: Always know your exit. Understanding how to convert crypto back to cash before you need to means no panic and no nasty surprises when it's time to take profit.

lessons.title: What is a DEX?
lessons.intro: A DEX (Decentralized Exchange) lets you trade crypto directly from your wallet — no account, no ID, no bank. Think of it as a vending machine instead of a cashier.

concepts.def: Decentralized Exchange. A platform where you trade directly from your wallet using smart contracts. No company controls it.
Centralized Exchange. A company (like Coinbase or Binance) that holds your crypto and processes trades. Requires an account and ID.
A self-executing program on the blockchain. When you trade on a DEX, a smart contract handles the swap automatically — no middleman.
Anyone can use a DEX without approval. No application, no waiting, no ID required. Just connect your wallet and trade.

Every action on a blockchain — a trade, a transfer — costs a small fee paid in that chain's native coin (SOL on Solana, ETH on Ethereum). It's called gas. Always keep a little of the native coin in your wallet to cover it.

questions.q: To use a DEX you need to create an account and verify your identity.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: DEXs are permissionless — just connect your wallet and trade. No signup, no ID, no approval needed. That's the beauty of DeFi.

questions.q: On a DEX, who processes your trade?
questions.answer: A smart contract on the blockchain
questions.why: Smart contracts automatically execute trades based on code. No human is involved — which means no one can stop your trade or freeze your funds.

questions.q: Which is safer from company bankruptcy?
questions.answer: DEX (Decentralized Exchange)
questions.why: FTX, Celsius, and others showed the risk of CEXs — when they fail, user funds disappear. A DEX can't go bankrupt because no company holds your funds.

lessons.title: What is Liquidity?
lessons.intro: Liquidity is basically how easy it is to buy or sell something without moving the price. More liquidity = smoother trades. Less liquidity = bigger price swings.

concepts.def: The amount of crypto available for trading. High liquidity = easy to buy/sell at stable prices. Low liquidity = prices jump around a lot.
A pot of two tokens locked in a smart contract that traders swap against. LP providers deposit tokens and earn fees from every trade.
When the price you actually get differs from the price you saw — because the market moved between you submitting the trade and it executing. Worse on low-liquidity tokens.
How much YOUR trade moves the price. A big buy in a small pool pushes the price up significantly.

questions.q: A token with $500 in liquidity is easier to trade without price impact than one with $500,000.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: More liquidity means your trade is a smaller percentage of the pool, causing less price impact. Low liquidity tokens can move dramatically on even small trades.

questions.q: What is slippage?
questions.answer: The difference between expected price and actual price you receive
questions.why: Slippage happens because prices change between when you submit a trade and when it executes. High slippage tolerance protects against failed transactions but exposes you to worse prices.

questions.q: You want to buy a token. Which pool is safer to trade in?
questions.answer: Pool with $100,000 liquidity
questions.why: More liquidity means less price impact on your trade. A $1,000 pool could move dramatically on a $100 buy. Always check liquidity before trading.

lessons.title: What is Market Cap?
lessons.intro: Price alone doesn't tell you how big a project is. A token at $0.000001 could be worth more overall than one at $100. Market cap is the real measure.

concepts.def: Price × Circulating Supply. This is the true size of a project. A $0.00001 token with 1 trillion supply has a $10M market cap.
The number of tokens actually available to trade right now. Locked or unvested tokens don't count.
Price × Total Supply (including tokens not yet released). Shows what the market cap would be if all tokens existed today.
A cheap price doesn't mean a good deal. Always check market cap. A $0.001 token with $1B market cap has less room to grow than a $10 token with $1M market cap.

questions.q: Token A costs $100 and Token B costs $0.001. Token A is definitely the bigger project.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: Price means nothing without supply context. Token B could have a trillion tokens in supply making it worth far more overall. Always check market cap, not just price.

questions.q: What is market cap?
questions.answer: Price multiplied by circulating supply
questions.why: Market cap = price × circulating supply. It's the most important metric for comparing project sizes. Two tokens at the same price can have wildly different market caps.

questions.q: A token has a $500K market cap. What does that mean?
questions.answer: The total value of all circulating tokens is $500K
questions.why: Market cap represents the current total value of all tokens in circulation at today's price. It's not money raised — it's market valuation.

lessons.title: Staying Safe in Crypto
lessons.intro: Crypto has no customer service hotline. No chargebacks. No refunds. Once your crypto is gone, it's gone. These basics will protect you from the most common traps.

concepts.def: When developers abandon a project and take all the liquidity, leaving holders with worthless tokens. Research the team and check if liquidity is locked.
Fake websites or DMs designed to steal your seed phrase or private key. Always verify URLs. Never click links from strangers.
Do Your Own Research. Never invest based on hype or someone else's advice alone. Read, verify, think critically.
If a token's mint authority isn't revoked, the creator can print unlimited new tokens and crash the price. Check this before buying.

questions.q: Someone DMs you on Telegram offering to help recover your wallet — you should share your seed phrase with them.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: NEVER. This is the most common scam in crypto. No legitimate person will ever need your seed phrase. Anyone asking for it is trying to steal everything in your wallet.

questions.q: Locked liquidity on a token means:
questions.answer: Devs can't pull the trading liquidity for a set time
questions.why: Locked liquidity is a major trust signal. It means devs physically cannot drain the pool during the lock period. Always check if liquidity is locked before buying.

questions.q: What does DYOR mean?
questions.answer: Do Your Own Research
questions.why: Do Your Own Research. In crypto, you are your own bank and your own analyst. Never rely solely on influencers, Telegram groups, or random advice. Verify everything yourself.

lessons.title: What Is Liquidity?
lessons.tagline: The foundation. Everything else builds on this.
lessons.intro: The foundation. Everything else builds on this.

sections.heading: The Basic Concept
sections.body:
Liquidity is simply how easily an asset can be bought or sold without dramatically changing its price.

Think of it like water. A deep ocean — you can throw a rock in and barely see a ripple. A shallow puddle — that same rock creates waves that hit every edge.

In crypto, the "water" is the money sitting in a trading pool. More water = more liquidity = less price impact when you trade.

HIGH LIQUIDITY POOL:
• Large trades execute near the quoted price
• Tight bid/ask spread
• Price is stable under normal trading volume

LOW LIQUIDITY POOL:
• Even small trades move the price significantly
• Wide spread
• Vulnerable to price manipulation

sections.heading: Why Liquidity Matters To YOU
sections.body:
Every time you swap a token you are interacting with a liquidity pool. The depth of that pool determines how good or bad your execution price is.

This is called SLIPPAGE — the difference between the price you expected and the price you actually got.

EXAMPLE:
You want to buy $100 worth of a token.
• Deep pool ($500K TVL) → slippage costs you only a few cents. You keep essentially all of your value.
• Shallow pool ($10K TVL) → slippage costs you around $2 — roughly 2%.

That may not sound like much on $100. But slippage scales fast with trade size: the same shallow pool that costs 2% on a $100 trade can cost a brutal double-digit percentage on a large one. That gap is money leaving your wallet — permanently, before the market even moves.

Hard Knocks Rule: ALWAYS check the pool liquidity before you buy. If you cannot find the pool depth, do not trade it.

sections.heading: Where Does Liquidity Come From?
sections.body:
In traditional finance, large institutions called market makers provide liquidity. They sit on both sides of the order book and pocket the spread.

In DeFi, YOU can be the market maker. Anyone can deposit tokens into a liquidity pool and earn fees from every trade that passes through it.

This is the fundamental promise of DeFi liquidity:
• Traders get access to markets 24/7
• Liquidity providers earn passive income from trading fees
• No middleman takes the spread

The people depositing tokens into pools are called Liquidity Providers — LPs. Every lesson in this lab is building toward making you a smarter one.

sections.heading: Liquidity Across Protocols
sections.body: The same concept exists on every DEX in crypto. The implementation differs but the fundamentals are identical. Master the concept on one protocol and you can walk into any of them.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.body:
These are the mistakes that cost people real money. Learn them here instead of the hard way.

❌ Trading illiquid tokens without checking pool depth first
❌ Setting slippage tolerance too high — bots will sandwich your transaction
❌ Setting slippage tolerance too low — your transactions will fail constantly
❌ Confusing token market cap with liquidity depth — they are not the same thing
❌ Assuming a token with a high price has deep liquidity — price and depth are independent
❌ Buying into a pool right after a large buy moved the price — you are the exit liquidity

questions.q: What is slippage?
questions.answer: Price gap between expected and actual execution
questions.why: Slippage is the difference between the price you saw when you submitted a trade and the price you actually got when it executed. It's caused by low liquidity and other trades happening at the same time.

questions.q: What happens when you make a large trade in a pool with very low liquidity?
questions.answer: Your trade moves the price significantly — you pay more than expected
questions.why: Low liquidity means your trade represents a large portion of the pool. The AMM formula pushes the price against you with every token you take out. This is called price impact — and it comes directly out of your pocket.

questions.q: Who provides liquidity in DeFi pools?
questions.answer: Anyone who deposits tokens earns fees
questions.why: In DeFi, anyone can be a liquidity provider. You deposit two tokens into a pool, earn a share of every trading fee generated, and can withdraw at any time. This is one of the most powerful concepts in all of DeFi.

questions.q: A pool has $500,000 in TVL. Another pool has $5,000 in TVL. Which gives better trade execution?
questions.answer: The $500,000 pool
questions.why: More liquidity always means less price impact for the same trade size. The $500,000 pool has 100x more depth so the same trade moves the price 100x less. Always trade in the deepest pool available.

questions.q: What is TVL?
questions.answer: Total Value Locked — the combined dollar value of tokens in a pool
questions.why: TVL stands for Total Value Locked. It represents the combined dollar value of all tokens currently sitting in a liquidity pool. Higher TVL generally means deeper liquidity and less slippage for traders.

questions.q: You set your slippage tolerance to 25% before a trade. What risk does this create?
questions.answer: MEV bots can sandwich your trade and extract value from your high tolerance
questions.why: High slippage tolerance is an invitation for sandwich attacks. MEV bots see your pending transaction, buy ahead of you to push the price up, let your trade execute at the worse price you accepted, then sell immediately after. Set slippage as low as practically possible.

questions.q: Which of these is a protocol-specific feature rather than a universal DeFi liquidity concept?
questions.answer: Orca Whirlpools tick spacing
questions.why: Impermanent loss, price impact, and slippage are universal concepts that apply to every AMM on every chain. Orca Whirlpools tick spacing is a specific implementation detail of Orca's concentrated liquidity system. Understanding the universal concepts first lets you navigate any protocol.

lessons.cluckVerdict: Liquidity is the foundation. Every single lesson in this lab builds on what you just learned. If you skipped something, go back. The LP Lab has no shortcuts and no sympathy for lazy students.

lessons.title: How AMMs Work
lessons.tagline: Every swap you have ever made went through one of these.
lessons.intro: Every swap you have ever made went through one of these.

sections.heading: What Is an AMM?
sections.body:
An Automated Market Maker is a smart contract that holds two tokens in a pool and automatically sets the price between them based on their ratio. There is no order book. There are no buyers and sellers being matched. Just math.

TRADITIONAL EXCHANGE (Order Book):
• Buyers post bids — prices they will pay
• Sellers post asks — prices they will accept
• A trade happens when a bid meets an ask
• Requires constant participation from market makers

AMM (Liquidity Pool):
• Two tokens sit in a pool — for example SOL and CLKN
• The ratio between them determines the price
• Anyone can swap against the pool at any time
• Price adjusts automatically with every trade

The AMM never sleeps. It never runs out of quotes. It never needs a counterparty. It is just math running on a blockchain 24 hours a day.

sections.heading: The x*y=k Formula
sections.body:
The most common AMM formula is the constant product formula. It looks like this:

x × y = k

Where:
• x = the amount of Token A in the pool
• y = the amount of Token B in the pool
• k = a constant — it never changes

EXAMPLE:
Pool has 1,000 SOL and 100,000,000 CLKN
k = 1,000 × 100,000,000 = 100,000,000,000

You want to buy some SOL by selling CLKN.
You add 1,000,000 CLKN to the pool.
New y = 101,000,000 CLKN

To keep k constant:
New x = k / new y = 100,000,000,000 / 101,000,000 = 990.099 SOL

You added 1,000,000 CLKN and received 1,000 - 990.099 = 9.9 SOL

The pool always maintains the constant product. This is why large trades relative to pool size move the price significantly — adding a lot to one side requires removing a lot from the other side to keep k the same.

sections.heading: How Price Moves
sections.body:
The price in an AMM is simply the ratio of the two tokens.

Price of SOL in CLKN = CLKN in pool / SOL in pool

STARTING STATE:
Pool: 1,000 SOL / 100,000,000 CLKN
Price: 100,000 CLKN per SOL

AFTER SOMEONE BUYS SOL (adds CLKN, removes SOL):
Pool: 990.099 SOL / 101,000,000 CLKN
New price: 102,010 CLKN per SOL

The price went up because there is now less SOL relative to CLKN in the pool. Every buy pushes price up. Every sell pushes price down.

This is why AMMs are called self-balancing — as the price in the pool drifts from the market price, arbitrageurs step in to buy the cheaper asset and sell the more expensive one, bringing the pool back into alignment. Arbitrage is what keeps AMM prices accurate.

sections.heading: Price Impact vs Slippage
sections.body:
These two terms are related but they are not the same thing. Confusing them costs people money.

PRICE IMPACT:
The change in price caused by your specific trade. It is deterministic — based purely on your trade size relative to the pool size. You can calculate it exactly before trading.

Large trade in small pool = high price impact
Small trade in large pool = low price impact

SLIPPAGE:
The difference between the price when you submitted the transaction and the price when it actually executed. Caused by other trades happening between submission and execution.

You set a slippage tolerance — the maximum you are willing to accept. If price moves more than your tolerance before your trade executes, the transaction fails.

TOO HIGH slippage tolerance: Your trade always goes through but sandwich bots exploit the gap to extract value from you.
TOO LOW slippage tolerance: Your trades fail constantly during volatile markets.

FINDING THE RIGHT TOLERANCE:
• Stable pairs and deep pools: 0.1-0.5%
• Normal pairs with good liquidity: 0.5-1%
• Volatile or illiquid tokens: 1-3%
• Never set above 5% unless you understand exactly what you are doing

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.body:
❌ Not checking price impact before a large trade — open DexScreener first
❌ Setting slippage too high on illiquid tokens — sandwich bots are watching
❌ Assuming the quoted price is what you will get — always check the minimum received
❌ Trading the same token in multiple transactions without checking pool state between them
❌ Ignoring the "minimum received" field — this is your actual worst-case execution
❌ Thinking failed transactions are free — on Solana a tx that lands in a block and fails still costs you the base fee AND the full priority fee. Retrying a failing swap ten times during congestion pays ten times

questions.q: In the AMM formula x*y=k, what does k represent?
questions.answer: A constant that never changes
questions.why: k is the constant product — the result of multiplying the two token reserves together. Every trade changes x and y but the product must remain k. This is what forces the price to move as trades happen.

questions.q: A pool has 500 SOL and 50,000,000 CLKN. You want to make a very large buy of SOL. What happens to the price of SOL?
questions.answer: Price goes up
questions.why: When you buy SOL you remove it from the pool and add CLKN. Less SOL relative to more CLKN means each SOL is worth more CLKN. The price of SOL goes up with every unit you buy. This is price impact — and the larger your trade relative to the pool, the more you pay above the starting price.

questions.q: What is the difference between price impact and slippage?
questions.answer: Price impact is your trade's effect on price. Slippage is from other trades while yours is pending.
questions.why: Price impact is deterministic — you can calculate it before trading based on your size vs pool size. Slippage is unpredictable — it depends on what other transactions execute before yours. Both cost you money but they come from different sources.

questions.q: Why do arbitrageurs keep AMM prices accurate?
questions.answer: They profit by trading the price difference — which brings prices back together
questions.why: When an AMM's price drifts from the real market price, arbitrageurs buy the cheaper asset in the AMM and sell it elsewhere (or vice versa) until the prices converge. They profit from the difference, and their activity is what keeps AMM prices aligned with the broader market.

questions.q: You want to swap $500 of SOL for CLKN. The pool has $50,000 TVL. Your friend wants to swap $50,000 of SOL in the same pool. Who experiences more price impact and why?
questions.answer: Your friend does — 100% of TVL in one trade vs your 1%
questions.why: Price impact scales with trade size relative to pool size. Your $500 trade is 1% of the $50,000 pool — minimal impact. Your friend's $50,000 trade equals the entire pool TVL — the x*y=k formula means they would drain so much of one token that the price moves dramatically against them. This is why large traders split trades or use pools with higher liquidity.

lessons.cluckVerdict: x times y equals k. Four characters. The foundation of hundreds of billions of dollars of DeFi volume. Now you know what actually happens when you hit swap.

lessons.title: Impermanent Loss
lessons.tagline: The #1 risk every LP must understand before deploying capital.
lessons.intro: The #1 risk every LP must understand before deploying capital.

sections.heading: What Is Impermanent Loss?
sections.body:
Impermanent loss is the difference in value between holding two tokens in your wallet versus providing them as liquidity in a pool.

When token prices change relative to each other, the AMM automatically rebalances — arbitrageurs buy the appreciating token from your pool until the ratio reflects the new market price. The result: you end up holding more of the token that went down and less of the one that went up.

It is called impermanent because if prices return to your entry ratio, the loss disappears entirely. It becomes permanent the moment you withdraw at a different price ratio than you entered.

SIMPLE EXAMPLE:
You deposit $1,000 into a SOL/USDC pool: $500 SOL + $500 USDC.
SOL doubles in price. The pool rebalances automatically.
If you had just held: $1,000 SOL + $500 USDC = $1,500
As an LP after rebalancing: approximately $1,414

Impermanent loss = $86 or 5.7%

The pool did not lose your money. The rebalancing mechanic redirected value away from you and toward the arbitrageurs who corrected the price.

sections.heading: The IL Table — Know These Numbers Cold
sections.body:
The relationship between price change and IL follows a predictable curve. Memorize the key data points.

PRICE CHANGE → IMPERMANENT LOSS:
1.25x price change → 0.6% IL
1.5x price change → 2.0% IL
2x price change → 5.7% IL
3x price change → 13.4% IL
4x price change → 20.0% IL
5x price change → 25.5% IL
10x price change → 42.5% IL

This applies whether the price goes up OR down by that multiple. A 2x move in either direction costs you the same 5.7%.

THE CRITICAL INSIGHT:
For low-volatility pairs the IL is manageable. For meme coins and volatile assets it is brutal. A 10x move — common in crypto — means you lose 42.5% of your position value compared to simply holding. Your fee income would need to be exceptional to overcome that.

sections.heading: When IL Matters and When It Does Not
sections.body:
IL is not always a problem. Context determines whether it is significant or irrelevant.

IL MATTERS WHEN:
• Tokens in the pair are uncorrelated — they move independently
• One token experiences a large price move while the other stays flat
• Fee income is low relative to the price divergence
• You are LPing meme coins or highly volatile assets

IL DOES NOT MATTER WHEN:
• Both tokens are highly correlated — they move together (BTC/ETH, SOL/jitoSOL)
• You are in a stablecoin pair — USDC/USDT has near-zero IL
• Fee income significantly exceeds the IL rate
• You believe prices will return to your entry ratio before you withdraw
• You are a long-term holder who would have held both tokens anyway

THE CORRELATED PAIR INSIGHT:
If you LP SOL/mSOL — both tokens track SOL price closely. When SOL goes up, both go up together. IL is minimal. This is why stablecoin pairs and liquid staking pairs are popular for conservative LPs.

sections.heading: IL vs Fee Income — The Real Calculation
sections.body:
The only number that actually matters is net return = fees earned minus IL — but you have to put both on the same clock first.

Fee APR is a RATE PER YEAR. Impermanent loss is NOT a rate — it is a one-off hit set purely by how far the price ratio moved, and it does not care whether that took a week or a decade. So "80% APR minus 5.7% IL = 74.3%" is only true if you actually held for a full year. Hold that same position for 30 days and you collect 80 × 30/365 = 6.6% in fees against the very same 5.7% IL — a net of +0.9%, not +74%.

HOW TO EVALUATE:
Step 1: Find the pool's 30-day fee APR on DexScreener or the protocol dashboard
Step 2: Estimate your expected IL based on the token pair's historical volatility
Step 3: Prorate the fee APR to how long you actually intend to hold — APR × days ÷ 365
Step 4: Subtract the estimated IL from THAT number, not from the headline APR
Step 5: Compare the result to simply holding the tokens

THE SHORTCUT THAT COSTS PEOPLE MONEY: subtracting an annual rate from a one-off loss. It flatters every short hold, and short holds are exactly where LPs get hurt — you eat the full IL of the move but only collect a sliver of the year's fees.

If net return after IL is higher than holding — LP position makes sense.
If net return after IL is lower than holding — you are better off just holding.

CLUCK'S FRAMEWORK: Never enter an LP position without running this calculation. The number of people who think they are earning yield while actually underperforming a simple hold is staggering.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.body:
❌ Providing liquidity to meme coin pairs without calculating expected IL
❌ Celebrating fee APR without subtracting IL — the gross number is meaningless
❌ Thinking IL only applies when prices go up — a 2x drop costs the same as a 2x rise
❌ Withdrawing immediately after a price move locks in IL permanently — sometimes waiting is correct
❌ Assuming stablecoin pairs have zero IL — they have very low IL but depeg events can cause real losses
❌ Not tracking your entry price ratio — you cannot calculate IL without knowing where you started

questions.q: Why is impermanent loss called 'impermanent'?
questions.answer: Loss disappears if prices return to entry — permanent only when you withdraw
questions.why: IL is impermanent because the AMM rebalancing is reversible. If the price ratio between the two tokens returns to exactly where it was when you deposited, your position value equals what you would have had by just holding. The loss only locks in permanently when you withdraw at a different ratio than you entered.

questions.q: SOL triples in price while USDC stays at $1. You are an LP in a SOL/USDC pool. What happened to your position?
questions.answer: The AMM rebalanced — you hold less SOL and more USDC, worth less than holding
questions.why: When SOL tripled, arbitrageurs bought SOL from your pool until the pool ratio reflected the new price. You sold SOL on the way up through the rebalancing mechanism. You now hold less of the appreciating asset (SOL) and more of the stable asset (USDC). This is IL — you underperformed a simple hold by approximately 13.4%.

questions.q: Which pair would have the LOWEST impermanent loss risk?
questions.answer: USDC/USDT
questions.why: USDC and USDT are both pegged to $1. Their price ratio almost never changes. IL requires price divergence between the two assets — if both assets always trade at the same price, IL is essentially zero. Stablecoin pairs are the safest from an IL perspective.

questions.q: You enter an LP position with $10,000. The pool earns 120% APR in fees over a year. But the token pair experienced a 4x price divergence causing 20% IL. What is your approximate net return?
questions.answer: 100% — fee APR minus IL rate
